title: CBP facial comparison at Dulles flags a French-passport impostor on day three; Congolese ID found in his shoe
summary: CBP's new facial comparison system at Dulles reported a mismatch for a man presenting a French passport on 22 Aug 2018; a Congolese ID was found in his shoe and he was returned to Brazil.
account: On 22 August 2018, the third day of facial comparison biometrics at Washington Dulles International Airport, a 26-year-old man arriving from Sao Paulo presented a French passport at primary inspection. CBP's release states that the officer used the facial comparison biometric technology, which confirmed the man was not a match to the passport; in secondary inspection officers found his authentic Republic of Congo identification card concealed in his shoe. CBP Area Port Director Daniel Mattina told NBC News the man was apprehended, processed and returned to Brazil. CBP called him the first impostor detected with the technology; CBP releases record a second (8 September 2018) and third (1 October 2018) impostor at Dulles and, by September 2021, more than 900 impostors nationally. The sources do not name the matching-algorithm vendor.
purpose: Verify arriving international travelers' identities by comparing a live photo with passport or visa photos in government holdings, to detect impostors and expedite entry.
system: CBP facial comparison biometric system (biometric entry/exit, Traveler Verification Service)
developer: Not named in the fetched sources
deployer: U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Office of Field Operations, Washington Dulles International Airport
taxonomy_note: Border impostor detection has no exact Trustible category; filed as organizational efficiency because the match replaced a manual photo comparison that, per NBC, might have passed with humans.

ratings.reason: An attempt to enter the United States on another person's genuine passport was stopped and the traveler removed; sources document no further threat beyond the document fraud.
CBP gained a verified first detection for a system then three days into use at Dulles; subsequent releases report repeated catches.

ai_role.statement: The facial comparison match (less than two seconds per CBP) produced the mismatch that triggered secondary inspection; the search and removal were human actions. The documentation is CBP's own release (deployer, not developer) plus NBC with a named CBP official. The algorithm vendor and the match threshold are not in the fetched sources, and CBP's '99% match rate' claim is unaudited here.
